title: Apply & Rebase Writing Suggestions

interviewer.approach: Two phases. (1) Conflict resolution in priority order: keep a list of accepted spans and accept a suggestion only if no accepted span overlaps it (start < e && s < end) or shares its start index. O(n^2) with a list, which is fine for n <= 1000; O(n log n) with a sorted structure (balanced tree or sorted list with bisect) that checks only the neighbours by start. (2) Sort the accepted suggestions by start and build the result in one left-to-right pass: copy text[pos:start], append the replacement, set pos = end; finally copy the tail. Building with a list/StringBuilder makes the pass O(len(text) + total replacement length). Applying replacements one at a time to a mutable string is a classic bug because later offsets shift; applying them right to left avoids the shift but still costs O(n * len) copies.
hints: Start with the conflict rule. Given two ranges [a, b) and [c, d), what's the condition for them to share a character? What about insertions, where start == end?
Once you know which suggestions survive, do their offsets still refer to the original text after you apply the first one?
Sort the accepted suggestions by start, then walk the original text once, copying the gaps and appending replacements.
pitfalls: Applying replacements one by one to the evolving string with the original offsets, so every later suggestion lands in the wrong place.
Using a closed-interval overlap test (start <= e && s <= end), which wrongly rejects adjacent ranges like [0, 2) and [2, 4).

Missing the insertion cases: two insertions at the same index, an insertion strictly inside a replacement, or an insertion at a replacement's start (all conflict), versus one at a replacement's end (fine).
Resolving conflicts by position order instead of priority order, or letting a skipped suggestion block later ones.
Repeated string concatenation in a loop, which is quadratic in some languages.

parts.title: Keep suggestions valid while the user types

interviewer.approach: Simulate: for each edit compute delta = insertedLength - (editEnd - editStart); for each live span, keep it when end <= editStart, shift both ends by delta when start >= editEnd, otherwise mark it [-1, -1]. Check the conditions in that order so an insertion edit at a span's start shifts the span and one at its end keeps it. O(n * m), fine for the constraints. Faster: sort spans by start; each edit affects a contiguous run of spans (binary search), and the shift applies to a suffix, so a lazy offset (Fenwick tree or a running offset when edits arrive in increasing position) brings it to O((n + m) log n). This is the core of operational transformation: a client's suggestions are transformed against concurrent local edits instead of being recomputed.
hints: Take one suggestion and one edit. Draw the three possible relationships between the two ranges.
What happens at the boundaries: a suggestion that ends exactly where the edit starts, or starts exactly where it ends? Pick the rule from the prompt and apply it in that order.
Each edit is in the coordinates of the text after earlier edits. If you update all spans after each edit, do you need anything else?
pitfalls: Applying all edits in original-text coordinates instead of sequentially.
Shifting only the start (or only the end) of a span.
Getting the boundary cases backwards: an insertion edit at a suggestion's start must shift it, at its end must keep it.
Relying by accident on [-1, -1] ending before every edit to keep dropped spans in place. It works, but a candidate should skip dropped spans explicitly or be able to say why it's safe.
Removing dropped suggestions from the output instead of returning [-1, -1] in place, which breaks the one-to-one order.

followUps: What are the time and space complexities of both parts? How would you make part 1's conflict check O(log n) per suggestion, and part 2 faster than O(spans × edits)?

Real text is UTF-16 in browsers, UTF-8 on many servers and grapheme clusters on screen. What goes wrong when a suggestion server and a browser extension disagree on what an 'index' is, and how would you avoid it?

Part 2 drops any suggestion that touches an edit. When could you keep it instead (for example, the user fixed the typo themselves, or typed inside a long sentence-level suggestion), and what would you need to know?

Suggestions are computed on the server for version N of the document while the client is already at version N + 3. How would you use part 2 to reconcile them, and how does this relate to operational transformation or CRDTs?
How would you test this so that a bug in offset handling can't ship to millions of users? What properties would you check with randomized tests?

interviewer.approach: Two related problems from a writing assistant. Part 1 is interval conflict resolution plus a single-pass string rebuild; part 2 is offset transformation under sequential edits. Expect part 1 in about 25 minutes. Strong candidates state the half-open overlap rule precisely, handle zero-length ranges deliberately, and test boundaries. In part 2 look for clean case analysis and for noticing that edits are sequential. Candidates with editor or browser-extension experience should connect part 2 to operational transformation and to index-unit mismatches (UTF-16 vs code points).

dimensions.name: Scrutinising the AI's offset and boundary logic
dimensions.signals: Checked the AI's overlap test against half-open ranges and zero-length insertions (same-start insertions, an insertion inside a replacement, at its start, at its end). Caught AI code that applies replacements to the evolving string with original offsets. In part 2, confirmed edits are applied sequentially and the keep/shift/drop checks run in the stated order, and that dropped spans stay [-1, -1] in place.

levels.1: Shipped AI code with shifting offsets or a closed-interval overlap test without noticing.
levels.2: Found the offset or boundary bugs only through failing hidden tests; couldn't say why they happened.
levels.3: Wrote targeted boundary tests (adjacent ranges, insertions at both ends of a range) before trusting the AI's code.
levels.4: Specified the overlap and rebase rules to the AI precisely up front, then reviewed its code line by line against them and explained the operational-transformation connection.

watchFor: Applying each replacement to the current string with the original offsets (or in priority order instead of position order), so later suggestions land in the wrong place.
Overlap tests with <= that treat adjacent ranges as conflicting, or tests that ignore zero-length insertions entirely.
Sorting suggestions by position before resolving conflicts, which throws away the priority order.
Part 2: treating every edit as if it were in original-text coordinates, or shifting a dropped [-1, -1] span.
Part 2: removing dropped suggestions from the result instead of returning [-1, -1] in place.
